one_liner: Lightweight JIT toolkit whose C11 front-end (c2m) compiles a header-free C function ~80x faster than gcc -O2.
what_it_does: MIR is a strongly-typed intermediate representation plus a lightweight JIT toolkit (interpreter + generator); C2MIR (`c2m`) is its C11 (+GCC extensions) front-end that compiles C source directly to MIR, then interprets or JIT-compiles it, without going through a full middle-end optimizer. It ships as a static/shared library plus a standalone `c2m` command-line compiler with gcc-like flags (-E/-c/-S/-o), and is meant to be embedded in an interpreter/runtime (the project's stated goal is CRuby/MRuby-style JITs) rather than swapped in as a project's system compiler.
how_it_is_fast: c2m uses a hand-written 4-pass pipeline (PEG-based recursive-descent parser, no yacc/flex, then context checking, then MIR generation) instead of a heavyweight preprocessor/parser/optimizer stack. MIR-generator itself runs only a short, deliberately minimal optimization pipeline (SSA built via Braun's algorithm, global value numbering, copy/dead-store/dead-code elimination, and a priority-based linear-scan register allocator with aggressive coalescing) instead of GCC's full middle end, keeping per-function compile overhead in the hundreds-of-microseconds range.
when_to_use: Embedding a C-based JIT inside an interpreter or dynamic-language runtime (the README's own target: CRuby/MRuby-style hot-path specialization)
Latency-sensitive compile paths where a single small function needs microsecond-scale turnaround rather than a whole translation unit
Lazy or basic-block-level code generation (-el/-eb) to defer codegen cost until a function or block is actually executed
Targeting x86-64, aarch64 (including Apple Silicon), ppc64le, s390x, or riscv64 on Linux/macOS and willing to vendor a small (~55K LOC), MIT-licensed compiler
Compiling small, self-contained C programs (no large #include trees) from the command line without installing GCC
when_not_to_use: Code needs VLAs, `_Complex`, `_Atomic`, or `_Thread_local` -- c2m's C11 subset omits them (c2mir/README.md lists them as unimplemented; issue #394 is an open request for `_Thread_local`)

Large, multi-file, header-heavy production builds -- the quoted ~80x is a single function with no #include files on an in-memory gcc run; a real build sees a much smaller gap per the record's own tradeoffs note
You need GDB-quality source-level debug info for compiled/JITted code -- still an open feature request (#442, opened Jul 2026)
Untrusted or adversarial C input -- several open heap-buffer-overflow/segfault issues in the parser and preprocessor (#353, #360, #362, #364, #365, #366) mean the front-end isn't hardened
You need generated code to match or beat gcc -O2 at runtime -- c2m -eg trades that away, running at ~91% geomean / ~92% on sieve of gcc -O2 speed

integration.form: static lib + shared lib + source-drop (also builds a standalone `c2m` compiler binary)
integration.dependencies: none to build (self-contained, builds with system gcc/clang); programs it compiles link libc/libm at runtime
integration.min_toolchain: C11/gnu11 to build MIR itself (GCC or Clang); c2m implements a C11 subset (no VLA/_Complex/_Atomic/_Thread_local) plus some GNU extensions
integration.platforms: x86-64, aarch64 (incl. Apple Silicon), ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 on Linux; x86-64/aarch64 macOS; Windows (MinGW/MSVC) is built by GNUmakefile though the README disclaimer only warranties the Linux/OSX/ppc64le/s390x/riscv64 CI-tested platforms
integration.thread_safety: MIR.md: 'You can use MIR functions in different threads without any synchronization if they work with different contexts in each thread' -- sharing one MIR_context across threads is not documented as safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- c2m is a working CLI C compiler with gcc-like flags (-E/-c/-S/-o), but it's a C11 subset intended for embedding a JIT, not a certified full-standard drop-in replacement for building arbitrary existing GCC-targeted projects

gotchas: No `_Thread_local`, `_Atomic`, VLA, or `_Complex` support in c2m (c2mir/README.md; issue #394 open)
Thread safety is per-MIR_context: separate contexts per thread need no synchronization, but sharing one context across threads isn't documented as safe
Using C as the JIT input (instead of building MIR IR directly via the API) can slow compilation up to 2x, per README
Multiple segfault/heap-buffer-overflow issues remain open in the parser/preprocessor path (e.g. #360, #362, #364, #365, #366), so malformed C input isn't guaranteed to fail safely
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MIR/c2m over TinyCC when you need an embeddable JIT library (interpret-or-generate, lazy per-function/per-block codegen, MIR IR you can also build directly via API) rather than just a fast standalone `cc`; TinyCC's ~9x-over-gcc number is for a traditional whole-program compile-and-link and doesn't offer c2m's lazy JIT interfaces. Neither zapcc (a caching Clang wrapper for incremental full C++ builds) nor cg_clif (a Rust/Cranelift backend) is a real alternative here -- both target different languages and build workflows entirely.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel i5-13600K (Fedora 37, GCC 12.3.1), c2m -eg compiled a single header-free C function (Eratosthenes sieve) in 336us vs gcc -O2's 27.1ms (~80x) and gcc -O0's 26.1ms (~77x, with gcc reading source from an in-memory filesystem to remove disk I/O); the resulting c2m-generated machine code then ran at ~92% of gcc -O2 speed on that same sieve and ~91% geomean (0.96 average) across 15 small C benchmarks from the repo's own suite.
status_note: Actively maintained -- commits and issue activity continue through Sep 2026 (last commit 2026-06-19, new issues as recent as #475 on 2026-09-03); MIT-licensed and small (~55K LOC per README) enough to vendor, with 'copyable' usability meaning a source/library integration rather than a packaged install.
